performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Witold Rowicki, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra
intro: Sviatoslav Richter plays the first movement, Allegro affettuoso, of Schumann’s Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 54, with Witold Rowicki and the Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra. The piano plays loud passages down the keyboard and also accompanies the clarinet, and the movement includes exchanges between soloist and orchestra.

relations.label: The opening group returns
relations.basis: The recapitulation restores the opening thematic group and its active bridge. These excerpts span that continuation in the exposition and recapitulation, matching the listening notes near 48 and 494 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.947, sustained 49 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 446.5 s (cache/form/schumann-piano-concerto-1.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

relations.label: The major-key theme comes home
relations.basis: The exposition’s C-major thematic restatement returns in A major during the recapitulation. The measured downward three-semitone shift agrees with that tonal change; these are excerpts inside the larger major-key groups. CENS diagonal mean 0.919, sustained 41 s, fixed pitch-class shift -3 semitones and time offset 441 s (cache/form/schumann-piano-concerto-1.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening: orchestral E and oboe theme
cues.text: The orchestra plays E in unison, and the piano descends in thick chords. An oboe then plays a tune beginning C–B–A–A. The piano takes it up.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, Clara Schumann edition, pp. 1–2; Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note confirms the unison E and ensuing oboe–piano exchange. https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboe theme and the name Chiara
cues.text: In German notation B♮ is H, so the oboe’s opening notes are C–H–A–A. Michael Steinberg read them as CHiArA, or Chiara, the Italian Clara that Schumann used in his prose and, as Chiarina, in Carnaval. The tune dominates the movement and returns to link it to the finale.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note: the first four notes of the oboe theme read C–H–A–A, Chiara, a name in Schumann’s prose writings and, as Chiarina, in Carnaval; the theme dominates the movement. https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54

cues.title: Second subject in C major
cues.text: The piano plays the main theme again in C major over a few pizzicato notes in the strings. At the Animato the clarinet takes the theme and the piano accompanies. Schumann built his second theme from the first.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, p. 6: a tempo, piano statement, pizzicato strings and clarinet at Animato. Calvin Dotsey describes the C-major return. https://houstonsymphony.org/schumann-piano-concerto/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Concert Fantasy, 1841
cues.text: In May 1841 Schumann wrote this music as a single-movement Concert Fantasy for Clara. Publishers and orchestras showed no interest. Four years later he revised it and added two movements, and the Fantasy became the first movement of his Piano Concerto.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note: composition 4–20 May 1841, unsuccessful attempts to place the Fantasy, and expansion in 1845. https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54 Schumann-Portal (Knechtges-Obrecht): begun in May 1841 after the First Symphony; his efforts to arrange a public performance and to find a publisher fail; reworked in early summer 1845 as the first movement of the concerto. https://www.schumann-portal.de/op-54-1267.html

cues.title: Letter to Clara Wieck, 1839
cues.text: In 1839 Schumann wrote to Clara that concertos were “hybrids of symphony, concerto, and big sonata”. He saw that he “can’t write a concerto for virtuosi” and would have to think of something else.
cues.evidence: Robert Schumann to Clara Wieck, 1839, in Michael Steinberg’s translation, Boston Symphony programme note: https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54 The German original and the letter’s date were not found (Weissweiler’s edition of the correspondence not opened).

cues.title: Andante espressivo in A♭ major
cues.text: Andante espressivo, in A♭ major and in 6/4. The clarinet has the melody over wide arpeggios in the piano, and the cellos hold sustained notes.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 14–16: Andante espressivo, A♭ major, 6/4, piano arpeggios, clarinet melody and sustained cellos. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/27/IMSLP51508-PMLP03738-RS16.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gewandhaus rehearsal, Leipzig, 1841
cues.text: Leipzig, 13 August 1841. At a Gewandhaus rehearsal of the “Spring” Symphony, Clara tried Robert’s new Fantasy with the orchestra for the first time. She wrote that in the empty hall “one can hear neither oneself nor the orchestra”, but she played it twice and “thought it magnificent!”
cues.evidence: Clara Schumann’s record of the rehearsal of 13 August 1841, in Berthold Litzmann, Clara Schumann: An Artist’s Life, trans. Grace E. Hadow, vol. 1 (1913), p. 326 n. 1: “But I played it twice, and thought it magnificent!” https://archive.org/details/claraschumannart01litz German in Schumann-Portal (Knechtges-Obrecht): “Ich spielte sie aber zwei mal, und fand sie herrlich!”, rehearsal at the Gewandhaus on 13 August 1841. https://www.schumann-portal.de/op-54-1267.html Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note gives 8 August and names Mendelssohn as conductor; both sources above give 13 August and name no conductor.

cues.title: Return of the opening piano flourish
cues.text: The piano flourish from the opening interrupts the slow duet. At Allegro, Tempo I the music returns to four beats in a bar. Flutes and strings reply to the descending piano figure, and the principal melody returns.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 16–18, rehearsal C: return to common time, Allegro (Tempo I), piano cascade and orchestral answers.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme, oboe
cues.text: After a ritardando, at Tempo I (rehearsal D), the oboe plays the quiet opening tune in A minor, supported by clarinets, bassoons and horns. The piano rests, then replies. The opening exchange returns without the first cascade.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, p. 23, rehearsal D: Tempo I, oboe-led wind theme and subsequent piano response.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Clara Schumann’s diary, 1845
cues.text: On 27 June 1845 Clara noted that Robert had added “a beautiful last movement” to his A minor Phantasie. She wrote that she had “always wanted a great bravura piece by him.” By 31 July the concerto was with the copyist, and she was “as happy as a king”.
cues.evidence: Clara Schumann’s entries of 27 June and 31 July 1845, in Litzmann, Clara Schumann: An Artist’s Life, trans. Hadow, vol. 1 (1913), p. 404; the quoted wording is Hadow’s: “Robert has added a beautiful last movement to his Phantasie in A minor … so that it has now become a concerto”, “I always wanted a great bravura piece by him”, “I am as happy as a king at the thought of playing it with the orchestra”. https://archive.org/details/claraschumannart01litz Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note quotes the June entry as “a big bravura piece”. https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54

cues.title: First performance, Dresden, 1845
cues.text: Clara Schumann gave the première of the complete concerto in Dresden on 4 December 1845. Ferdinand Hiller, the work’s dedicatee, conducted.
cues.evidence: Première date, soloist, conductor and dedication: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54 ; Schumann-Portal (Knechtges-Obrecht): première on 4 December 1845 in Dresden, Clara soloist, conducted by the dedicatee Ferdinand Hiller. https://www.schumann-portal.de/op-54-1267.html

cues.title: Review of the Leipzig performance, 1846
cues.text: The Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, the journal Schumann founded in 1834 and left in 1844, reviewed the first Leipzig performance, given on New Year’s Day 1846. The critic F.W.M. found the first movement harder to grasp than the other two, because soloist and orchestra exchange so many phrases.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, Boston Symphony programme note, on the review by F.W.M. in the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik; RIPM introduction on the journal’s founding in 1834 and Schumann’s resignation on 1 July 1844. https://www.bso.org/works/schumann-piano-concerto-in-a-minor-opus-54 ; https://ripm.org/assets/files/introductions/NZM1834-1844introEnglish.pdf

cues.title: Cadenza
cues.text: The orchestra stops and the piano plays alone. Schumann wrote out the cadenza in full. The two hands imitate each other and move into chords, then into long trills, and the left hand plays a melody beneath a high trill.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 35–36: solo lead-in, written Cadenza, imitative figures, chordal writing and Un poco Andante with sustained trills.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing Allegro molto, A minor
cues.text: The closing Allegro molto sets the familiar tune in two-beat bars. Woodwinds play it over quick figuration in the piano, and the strings punctuate the phrases. The music returns repeatedly to A minor and ends with loud chords for the full orchestra.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 37–41: Allegro molto in 2/4, wind theme, piano figuration and final A-minor cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Ritardando to the C major melody
transitions.to: A′ · The theme in C major
transitions.how: The connecting passage slows with a ritardando. At a tempo the piano plays the principal melody in C major, and the strings add a short pizzicato chord. At Animato the clarinet takes over the melody and the piano accompanies.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, p. 6: ritardando, a tempo, pizzicato strings, then Animato with clarinet melody. C-major return also described by Calvin Dotsey. https://houstonsymphony.org/schumann-piano-concerto/

transitions.title: Into the A♭ major Andante espressivo
transitions.from: A′ · The theme in C major
transitions.to: A″ · Piano and clarinet in A♭ major
transitions.how: The orchestral fanfare dies away and the metre broadens to 6/4. The music moves to A♭ major, marked Andante espressivo, and the piano plays spread arpeggios over a held A♭ in the cellos. A few bars later the clarinet takes up the melody. Trumpets, timpani and double basses rest.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 13–14: end of the tutti, Andante espressivo in A♭ and 6/4; cello pedal and clarinet response.

transitions.title: Return of the descending flourish after A♭ major
transitions.from: A″ · Piano and clarinet in A♭ major
transitions.to: Dev · Return of the opening cascade
transitions.how: The A♭ major duet slows, then Allegro, Tempo I restores common time. The piano’s descending flourish returns with an orchestral accent. Flutes, violins and lower strings follow with the same falling motion. The quiet arpeggios of the A♭ major section are replaced by loud scales and chords.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, p. 16, rehearsal C and the following orchestral answer.

transitions.title: Oboe theme in A minor at Tempo I
transitions.from: Dev · Return of the opening cascade
transitions.to: A · Oboe theme returns in A minor
transitions.how: A ritardando stretches the last piano figures over held wind chords and a quiet timpani roll. At Tempo I the oboe begins the A minor theme, accompanied by clarinets, bassoons and horns. Strings and piano stop after the first chord, and the winds finish the phrase alone.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, p. 23, last bars before rehearsal D and the eight-bar wind statement.

transitions.title: From the reprise into the cadenza
transitions.from: A′ · The theme in A major
transitions.how: The A major reprise ends with a sharp orchestral accent. The piano continues alone, playing runs up and down before a ritardando. Schumann’s written cadenza follows. Its first figures pass between the hands and thicken into full chords before the long trills.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 35–36: solo lead-in, ritardando and Cadenza.

transitions.title: Two-beat phrases in the Allegro molto coda
transitions.how: This join falls within the coda, marked Allegro molto and written in 2/4. The woodwinds play a shortened form of the theme over quick figures in the piano, and the strings reply with short phrases. Accents and rising runs bring the full ensemble back together, and the harmony moves towards the close in A minor.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, pp. 37–41, Allegro molto coda. This join marks the later build within the coda.

source.title: Schumann, Piano Concerto, Op. 54, I. Allegro affettuoso, full score (Breitkopf & Härtel; Clara Schumann edition)
source.locator: First movement, pp. 1–41: oboe theme on p. 1; C-major piano and clarinet on p. 6; Andante espressivo on pp. 14–16; return on p. 23; cadenza on p. 36; coda on pp. 37–41.

timeline.note: The orchestra plays a single E; the piano follows with a descending run of chords.
The oboe plays the A-minor theme with the other winds; the piano answers.
The violins’ rising and falling figure passes through a fuller orchestral passage, with active piano writing.
The piano states the tune in C major; the clarinet answers above quiet strings and piano accompaniment.
Winds, brass and strings play the connecting figure as a fanfare before the Andante.
Piano arpeggios spread above held cellos; clarinet and piano share the A♭-major melody.
The piano cascade returns; flutes and strings answer with falling scales.
The oboe brings back the A-minor theme, with clarinets, bassoons and horns beneath it; the piano answers.
The connecting passage returns, with violin figures, busy piano writing and woodwind answers.
The piano brings the tune back in A major; clarinet and quiet strings join the exchange.
The piano plays the written cadenza alone, with answering phrases, thick chords and long trills.
Oboes, clarinets and bassoons play the shortened theme above piano trills and quick figures; the strings add short answers.
Piano runs and accented orchestral chords lead towards A minor; trumpets and timpani join in the final bars.

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
